items.prompt: Which component executes instructions in a computer?
items.answer: CPU
items.explanation: The CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions; peripherals handle input or output.

items.prompt: Which memory usually loses its contents when power is removed?
items.answer: RAM
items.explanation: RAM is volatile working memory. Persistent storage retains data without normal operating power.

items.prompt: Which device is primarily an input device?
items.answer: Scanner
items.explanation: A scanner converts physical documents or images into digital input.

items.prompt: Which device is primarily an output device?
items.answer: Monitor
items.explanation: A monitor presents processed information to the user.

items.prompt: What is the basic unit of binary information?
items.answer: Bit
items.explanation: A bit has two possible values, conventionally written as 0 and 1.

items.prompt: How many bits make one byte?
items.explanation: A byte contains eight bits in the standard convention used by modern computers.

items.prompt: What is the decimal value of binary 1010?
items.explanation: Read place values from right to left: 0×1 + 1×2 + 0×4 + 1×8 = 10.

items.prompt: Why is cache memory useful?
items.answer: It reduces access time for frequently used data
items.explanation: Cache keeps frequently needed data close to the processor, reducing slower memory accesses.

items.prompt: Which storage device normally has no moving mechanical parts?
items.answer: SSD
items.explanation: An SSD uses electronic memory rather than rotating platters and a moving read/write head.

items.prompt: What is an operating system mainly responsible for?
items.answer: Managing hardware resources and application execution
items.explanation: An operating system coordinates processes, memory, files and access to devices.

items.prompt: Which filename extension commonly denotes a PDF document?
items.answer: .pdf
items.explanation: PDF is a document format; the other extensions commonly identify a spreadsheet, audio or image.

items.prompt: What does a folder provide in a file system?
items.answer: A way to organize files and subfolders
items.explanation: Folders organize file paths; they do not by themselves improve security or hardware performance.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a backup?
items.answer: Keeping a recoverable copy of important data
items.explanation: A backup supports recovery after loss or damage. It should be checked and stored separately where appropriate.

items.prompt: Which action changes a file's location rather than making another copy?
items.answer: Move
items.explanation: Moving places the file at another path; copying leaves a second instance.

items.prompt: What is mail merge used for?
items.answer: Creating personalized documents from one template and a data source
items.explanation: Mail merge inserts fields such as a recipient name into a common letter or label template.

items.prompt: What does a header usually contain?
items.answer: Content repeated at the top of pages
distractors: Only the last word in a document
items.explanation: Headers commonly hold repeated titles or identifiers. Section settings can change which pages share a header.

items.prompt: Which alignment distributes text between both left and right margins?
items.answer: Justified
items.explanation: Justified paragraphs adjust spacing to align most lines with both margins.

items.prompt: Why are heading styles useful?
items.answer: They give documents structure and support automatic tables of contents
distractors: They force every page into landscape
They protect documents from all viruses
items.explanation: Semantic heading styles support consistent formatting, navigation and generated contents.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of Find and Replace?
items.answer: Locating specified text and optionally substituting another text
items.explanation: Find identifies matching text. Replace can change those matches; review scope before using Replace All.

items.prompt: What does Track Changes help reviewers see?
items.answer: Recorded edits to document content
distractors: All websites visited by the author
Every printed document in the office
items.explanation: Tracked edits make proposed insertions and deletions visible for review and acceptance or rejection.

items.prompt: What identifies a cell at column B and row 7?
items.answer: B7
items.explanation: In A1 notation, the column letter precedes the row number.

items.prompt: Which formula adds cells A1 through A5?
items.answer: =SUM(A1:A5)
items.explanation: SUM adds numeric values in the selected range; COUNT counts numeric entries.

items.prompt: What does =AVERAGE(2,4,6) return?
items.explanation: The arithmetic mean is the total 12 divided by the three values.

items.prompt: Which reference locks both column and row when copied?
items.explanation: A dollar sign before both coordinates makes both parts absolute.

items.prompt: Which reference locks the row but lets the column change?
items.explanation: B$3 is mixed: row 3 stays fixed while the column can adjust.

items.prompt: What does =IF(5>3,"Yes","No") return?
items.answer: Yes
items.explanation: IF evaluates the condition, returning its second argument when true and its third when false.

items.prompt: What does COUNT usually count in a range?
items.answer: Cells containing numeric values
items.explanation: COUNT counts numbers. COUNTA counts non-empty cells and COUNTBLANK counts blank cells.

items.prompt: Which function selects the largest numeric value in a range?
items.answer: MAX
items.explanation: MAX returns the greatest numeric value; MIN returns the least.

items.prompt: Why can a chart be misleading if its axis is truncated?
items.answer: It can exaggerate apparent differences
distractors: It changes the actual source values
items.explanation: An altered axis scale changes visual comparisons; inspect labels and units before interpreting.

items.prompt: What does a slide master help manage?
items.answer: Common slide layout and formatting
items.explanation: A slide master provides shared design elements and layout settings across slides.

items.prompt: How does a transition differ from an animation?
items.answer: A transition controls movement between slides
distractors: A transition changes only file permissions
An animation always affects all slides
items.explanation: Transitions act between slides; animations affect objects or content within a slide.

items.prompt: What does LAN stand for?
items.answer: Local Area Network
items.explanation: A LAN connects devices within a limited geographic area, such as a building.

items.prompt: What does DNS primarily do?
items.answer: Resolve domain names to network addresses
items.explanation: DNS helps clients locate hosts using domain names rather than requiring users to memorize numeric addresses.

items.prompt: Which protocol is associated with encrypted web connections?
items.answer: HTTPS
items.explanation: HTTPS carries HTTP over an encrypted connection; encryption does not prove the site's honesty.

items.prompt: How long is an IPv4 address?
items.answer: 32 bits
items.explanation: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.

items.prompt: How long is an IPv6 address?
items.answer: 128 bits
items.explanation: IPv6 provides a larger address space using 128-bit addresses.

items.prompt: What is a router mainly used for?
items.answer: Forwarding packets between networks
items.explanation: Routers choose paths and forward traffic between connected networks.

items.prompt: What does a URL identify?
items.answer: The address of a resource
items.explanation: A URL specifies how and where a resource can be accessed, often using a scheme, host and path.

items.prompt: Which email field hides recipients from other recipients?
items.answer: BCC
items.explanation: Blind carbon copy recipients are not displayed in the ordinary recipient list to others.

items.prompt: Which protocol is mainly associated with sending email?
items.answer: SMTP
items.explanation: SMTP handles email submission and transfer; IMAP and POP3 are used for retrieval.

items.prompt: Which protocol supports keeping email folders synchronized with a server?
items.answer: IMAP
items.explanation: IMAP supports server-based mailbox access and synchronization across clients.

items.prompt: What is phishing?
items.answer: Deceptive messages that try to obtain information or provoke unsafe actions
items.explanation: Phishing impersonates trusted parties. Check the sender, destination and requested action independently.

items.prompt: What distinguishes ransomware?
items.answer: It blocks access to data or systems and demands payment
items.explanation: Ransomware commonly encrypts files or otherwise prevents access. Backups and updates reduce recovery risk.

items.prompt: What is a firewall primarily designed to do?
items.answer: Filter network traffic according to rules
items.explanation: A firewall permits or blocks traffic using configured rules; it is one part of security.

items.prompt: Why is multi-factor authentication useful?
items.answer: It requires more than one type of authentication evidence
distractors: It removes the need for account recovery
It guarantees phishing can never occur
items.explanation: Combining independent factors makes a stolen password alone less useful to an attacker.

items.prompt: Which practice is best for different online accounts?
items.answer: Use unique strong passwords
distractors: Store passwords in a shared document without controls
items.explanation: Unique passwords limit the damage when one account's credentials are compromised.

items.prompt: What is the principle of least privilege?
items.answer: Grant only the access needed for a task
items.explanation: Least privilege reduces unnecessary access and limits the impact of mistakes or compromised accounts.

items.prompt: Why should software updates be installed from trusted sources?
items.answer: They may fix known vulnerabilities and bugs
distractors: They allow passwords to be removed
items.explanation: Trusted updates can address security defects. Read material compatibility changes before applying them.

items.prompt: Which action is safest for an unexpected attachment?
items.answer: Verify its source and purpose before opening
items.explanation: Unexpected files can contain malicious code. Independent verification is safer than trusting appearance alone.

items.prompt: What does alternative text for an informative image provide?
items.answer: A textual description for people who cannot see the image
distractors: A substitute for every caption in every context
items.explanation: Alt text communicates the image's purpose or information to assistive technology users.

items.prompt: Which example mainly illustrates growth rather than a qualitative developmental change?
items.answer: An increase in a child's height
distractors: A new strategy for solving a puzzle
items.explanation: Growth concerns measurable physical change; development includes changes in functioning and capabilities.

items.prompt: Why should teachers avoid assuming all children develop at an identical pace?
items.answer: Development varies across individuals and domains
distractors: Every child learns only through rewards
items.explanation: Development shows broad patterns but rates and experiences differ; instruction should respond to evidence from learners.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes heredity and environment?
items.answer: Both interact in development
items.explanation: Inherited characteristics and experiences interact rather than acting as completely isolated explanations.

items.prompt: Which practice supports child-centred education?
items.answer: Planning activities around learners' needs and participation
items.explanation: Child-centred teaching makes learners active participants while the teacher provides purposeful guidance.

items.prompt: A child solves a task with help but cannot yet solve it alone. Which concept is most relevant?
items.answer: Zone of proximal development
items.explanation: Vygotsky's ZPD concerns the difference between independent performance and performance with suitable guidance.

items.prompt: What is scaffolding in learning?
items.answer: Temporary support adjusted and reduced as competence grows
distractors: Permanent completion of all work by the teacher
items.explanation: Scaffolding supports a learner during a task and is gradually withdrawn as independent competence develops.

items.prompt: Which task is associated with Piaget's idea of conservation?
items.answer: Recognizing that quantity remains despite a change of shape
items.explanation: Conservation involves understanding that transformations in appearance need not change quantity.

items.prompt: A young child assumes everyone sees the scene exactly as they do. Which term describes this?
items.answer: Egocentrism
items.explanation: In this developmental context, egocentrism means difficulty coordinating another person's perspective, not selfishness.

items.prompt: What does object permanence mean?
items.answer: Understanding that an object exists even when out of sight
items.explanation: Object permanence is the understanding of continued existence without immediate perception.

items.prompt: Which ability is especially associated with formal operational reasoning?
items.answer: Reasoning about hypothetical possibilities
items.explanation: Formal operational reasoning includes abstract and hypothetical reasoning; teaching still depends on the individual task and learner.

items.prompt: Which example illustrates learning through observation?
items.answer: A pupil adopts a strategy after watching a peer model it
items.explanation: Observational learning involves attending to and learning from a model, not merely physical change.

items.prompt: What is positive reinforcement?
items.answer: Adding a consequence that increases the likelihood of a behaviour
items.explanation: Reinforcement is defined by its effect on behaviour; positive refers to adding a consequence.

items.prompt: How does negative reinforcement differ from punishment?
items.answer: It increases behaviour by removing an aversive condition
distractors: It means giving a low mark
It means publicly criticizing a child
items.explanation: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to strengthen behaviour. Punishment aims to reduce behaviour.

items.prompt: What is intrinsic motivation?
items.answer: Engaging because the activity itself is interesting or satisfying
distractors: Studying only for a cash prize
Working only to avoid a fine
Copying solely to gain a reward
items.explanation: Intrinsic motivation arises from interest or satisfaction in the activity rather than a separate external reward.

items.prompt: Which classroom practice is consistent with constructivism?
items.answer: Eliciting prior ideas and helping learners test and revise them
items.explanation: Constructivist approaches connect new understanding with prior knowledge through active sense-making.

items.prompt: What is meaningful transfer of learning?
items.answer: Applying understanding to a new relevant situation
items.explanation: Transfer occurs when knowledge or strategies are used beyond the exact setting in which they were learned.

items.prompt: What is metacognition?
items.answer: Awareness and regulation of one's own thinking and learning
items.explanation: Planning, monitoring comprehension and evaluating strategies are metacognitive processes.

items.prompt: A learner says an answer is wrong but cannot explain why. What should the teacher probe?
items.answer: The learner's reasoning and evidence
distractors: Only the colour of the notebook
items.explanation: Probing reasons makes misconceptions visible and supports conceptual understanding.

items.prompt: Which activity encourages problem solving rather than mechanical copying?
items.answer: Comparing multiple strategies for an unfamiliar task
distractors: Copying a solved answer ten times
items.explanation: Comparing strategies promotes reasoning about conditions, efficiency and justification.

items.prompt: Why can an error be useful during instruction?
items.answer: It can reveal a learner's current model or misconception
distractors: It proves the learner can never improve
items.explanation: An error is evidence to interpret, not a diagnosis of permanent inability or lack of effort.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of formative assessment?
items.answer: Using evidence during learning to improve the next steps
items.explanation: Formative assessment guides feedback and instructional adjustments while learning is still in progress.

items.prompt: Which example is primarily summative assessment?
items.answer: An end-of-course test used to report achievement
distractors: An exit ticket used to plan tomorrow's lesson
A diagnostic discussion before a unit
items.explanation: Summative assessment summarizes achievement at the end of a defined period; purpose distinguishes assessment types.

items.prompt: Why is a diagnostic assessment useful before teaching a unit?
items.answer: It identifies existing knowledge and specific gaps
distractors: It guarantees every learner has identical needs
It eliminates the need for feedback
items.explanation: Diagnosis helps plan suitable starting points and targeted support.

items.prompt: Which feedback is most actionable?
items.answer: Explain your grouping rule and check it against the third example
items.explanation: Actionable feedback identifies the issue and a concrete next step rather than labelling the person.

items.prompt: What does a rubric describe?
items.answer: Criteria and performance levels for judging work
distractors: Only the date of an examination
items.explanation: A rubric makes evaluation criteria and levels explicit, supporting consistency and feedback.

items.prompt: What does validity concern in an assessment?
items.answer: Whether evidence supports the intended interpretation and use
distractors: Only whether the paper is colourful
items.explanation: An assessment should support the inference being made. A spelling test alone cannot establish mathematical understanding.

items.prompt: What does reliability mainly concern?
items.answer: Consistency of measurement under relevant conditions
distractors: The length of a student's name
items.explanation: Reliable measurement produces sufficiently consistent results; reliability alone does not ensure valid interpretation.

items.prompt: Which practice supports self-assessment?
items.answer: Learners comparing work with explicit criteria and identifying next steps
distractors: Making peers responsible for all grades
items.explanation: Self-assessment develops monitoring when learners understand criteria and use evidence from their work.

items.prompt: What is inclusive education primarily concerned with?
items.answer: Removing barriers to participation and learning
distractors: Giving every learner the same support regardless of need
items.explanation: Inclusion addresses barriers through accessibility, support and participation in a shared learning community.

items.prompt: Which difficulty is most directly associated with dyslexia?
items.answer: Persistent difficulties in accurate or fluent word reading
items.explanation: Dyslexia concerns reading-related difficulties; identification requires appropriate assessment rather than one classroom error.

items.prompt: Which difficulty is most directly associated with dyscalculia?
items.answer: Significant difficulty understanding and working with numbers
items.explanation: Dyscalculia concerns numerical learning. Support should respond to assessed needs without labelling from a single task.

items.prompt: Which support can help a learner with low vision access a worksheet?
items.answer: Accessible digital text or appropriately enlarged high-contrast print
distractors: Publicly comparing the learner with classmates
items.explanation: Accessible formats improve participation while maintaining learning goals; suitable adjustments vary by learner.

items.prompt: How should a teacher respond to a gender stereotype in a textbook?
items.answer: Discuss and challenge it using diverse examples
distractors: Present it as a biological rule
Assign tasks only according to the stereotype
items.explanation: Teachers can help learners question stereotypes and see varied roles and capabilities.

items.prompt: A learner speaks a different home language. Which response best supports participation?
items.answer: Use multilingual resources and connect familiar language with new concepts
distractors: Punish the use of the home language
items.explanation: Home languages are learning resources. Language difference should not be treated as an intellectual deficit.

items.prompt: Why is a single score insufficient to describe a learner fully?
items.answer: Abilities, contexts and assessment conditions are multidimensional
distractors: One test measures all future success
items.explanation: Different evidence is needed for different capabilities; one score cannot capture the whole learner.

items.prompt: What does differentiated instruction aim to do?
items.answer: Adjust pathways and support while pursuing appropriate learning goals
distractors: Give the same task in exactly the same way to everyone
items.explanation: Differentiation responds to readiness and needs through suitable tasks, resources and support.

items.prompt: Which activity best supports collaborative learning?
items.answer: A shared task with purposeful roles and individual participation
items.explanation: Collaboration involves interdependence and participation, rather than simply sitting together.

items.prompt: Which teacher question best encourages explanation?
items.answer: What evidence supports your answer?
distractors: Who can repeat my sentence fastest?
items.explanation: Questions about evidence and reasons reveal thinking and encourage justification.

items.prompt: How should a teacher use a learner's alternative conception?
items.answer: Elicit it and design evidence-based activities that test it
distractors: Treat it as proof of dishonesty
items.explanation: Learning can involve revising an existing conception; carefully chosen examples help reveal its limits.

items.prompt: What is remedial teaching best based on?
items.answer: A diagnosed difficulty and targeted instruction
items.explanation: Remediation should address the particular barrier and check whether the support improves learning.

items.prompt: Why should a teacher vary examples across contexts?
items.answer: To help learners identify the underlying concept rather than surface features
distractors: To eliminate the need for explanation
items.explanation: Varied examples and non-examples help separate a rule from incidental details.

items.prompt: What is the strongest reason to use concrete materials in early mathematics?
items.answer: To connect actions and representations with mathematical ideas
items.explanation: Concrete representations support understanding when teachers explicitly connect them to ideas and symbols.

items.prompt: Which use of a portfolio supports assessment?
items.answer: Selecting work over time and reflecting on progress using criteria
items.explanation: A portfolio can show development across tasks and revisions when selection and reflection are purposeful.

items.prompt: What is a constructive response to an adolescent exploring different identities?
items.answer: Offer respectful guidance and opportunities for reflection
distractors: Assume every adolescent has the same experience
items.explanation: Identity exploration benefits from supportive relationships, boundaries and opportunities to reason about choices.

items.prompt: Which teacher response promotes a safe classroom during adolescence?
items.answer: Address bullying promptly and encourage respectful participation
items.explanation: A safe environment protects dignity and supports participation without humiliation.

items.prompt: Why can peer relationships matter during adolescence?
items.answer: They can influence belonging, identity and behaviour
distractors: They completely replace all family influence
items.explanation: Peers can matter significantly, but family, school, culture and individual circumstances also influence development.

items.prompt: What distinguishes a hypothesis from an unsupported conclusion?
items.answer: A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation
distractors: A hypothesis is always proved true
A hypothesis is simply a final mark
items.explanation: A hypothesis states a proposition that can be examined through evidence; results may support or challenge it.

items.prompt: What is a sample in research?
items.answer: A selected subset of the population being studied
items.explanation: A sample is drawn from a defined population. Its selection affects what conclusions can reasonably be generalized.

items.prompt: Why is informed consent important in educational research?
items.answer: Participants should understand relevant information and participate voluntarily
distractors: It permits any undisclosed data use
items.explanation: Ethical participation requires appropriate information and choice; consent does not remove other ethical responsibilities.

items.prompt: Why should a researcher distinguish correlation from causation?
items.answer: Association alone does not establish that one factor causes another
items.explanation: Confounding or reverse causation can explain an association; causal claims need an appropriate design and evidence.

items.prompt: What is assimilation in Piaget's framework?
items.answer: Interpreting a new experience using an existing schema
distractors: Changing a schema to fit contradictory evidence
items.explanation: Assimilation fits experience into an existing schema; accommodation modifies the schema when needed.

items.prompt: What is accommodation in Piaget's framework?
items.answer: Modifying a schema to account for a new experience
items.explanation: Accommodation changes a mental structure when the existing one does not adequately explain experience.

items.prompt: Why are several kinds of assessment evidence useful?
items.answer: They provide a broader picture of learning than a single task
distractors: They guarantee every learner gets the same mark
items.explanation: Combining observations, explanations and tasks can reveal different aspects of understanding.

items.prompt: An adolescent asks for more choice in a class project. Which response best supports growing autonomy?
items.answer: Offer bounded choices with clear goals and responsibility
distractors: Reject all choices solely because of age
Complete the whole project for the learner
items.explanation: Autonomy develops through meaningful choices, guidance and accountability, rather than either total control or absence of boundaries.

items.prompt: Why should a teacher avoid assuming that all adolescents develop at the same rate?
items.answer: Development varies across individuals and domains
distractors: Every learner has an identical timetable
One test measures every form of development
items.explanation: Physical, social, emotional and cognitive development need not progress uniformly or identically in every learner.

items.prompt: A learner seems confident with friends but hesitant in public presentations. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
items.answer: Performance and confidence can vary by context
distractors: The learner has no knowledge in any subject
The learner must be deliberately dishonest
Confidence is fixed and cannot change
items.explanation: Context, familiarity and perceived social evaluation can affect participation; one behaviour should not define the learner globally.

items.prompt: Which classroom practice can reduce embarrassment when adolescents make mistakes?
items.answer: Treat errors as information for learning and respond respectfully
distractors: Display a public list of the least capable learners
items.explanation: A respectful environment makes it easier to attempt challenging work and use feedback without fear of humiliation.

items.prompt: How should a teacher respond when peer exclusion is reported?
items.answer: Listen, document concerns and use the school's safeguarding and inclusion procedures
distractors: Require the learner to solve every problem alone
items.explanation: Peer exclusion should be taken seriously and addressed through appropriate school procedures rather than public humiliation or unsupported conclusions.

items.prompt: Which arrangement makes collaborative work more accountable?
items.answer: Clear roles, shared goals and evidence of individual contribution
items.explanation: Structure supports participation and prevents group work from hiding unequal contributions or understanding.

items.prompt: Why can peer feedback be useful for adolescent learners?
items.answer: It can expose alternative explanations and support revision when criteria are clear
distractors: Peers are always more accurate than every teacher
It removes the need to learn the content
It should consist only of popularity votes
items.explanation: Feedback is useful when specific, respectful and linked to evidence, rather than status or friendship.

items.prompt: A student disagrees with a classroom rule. Which response encourages reasoned judgment?
items.answer: Invite reasons and discuss the rule's purpose and fair application
distractors: Treat every disagreement as proof of inability
Change the rule randomly without explanation
items.explanation: Adolescents can practise examining reasons, consequences and fairness within clear expectations.

items.prompt: Which task especially supports hypothetical reasoning?
items.answer: Predict outcomes under different stated assumptions and justify them
distractors: Repeat an answer without considering conditions
items.explanation: Hypothetical reasoning explores possible conditions and consequences while keeping assumptions explicit.

items.prompt: Why should abstract ideas still be supported by examples in secondary classes?
items.answer: Examples can connect unfamiliar concepts to prior knowledge and reveal misconceptions
distractors: Adolescents never benefit from concrete representations
Every abstract concept is already understood at a fixed age
items.explanation: Age alone does not guarantee mastery; examples and varied representations help learners build and test understanding.

items.prompt: What is metacognitive monitoring during study?
items.answer: Checking one's understanding and deciding whether a strategy is working
items.explanation: Monitoring lets learners identify gaps and adjust strategies rather than rely only on how familiar material feels.

items.prompt: Which study action best supports retrieval practice?
items.answer: Attempt an answer from memory, then check and correct it
distractors: Look at the answer while copying every time
items.explanation: Retrieval requires bringing information to mind; checking afterward helps correct errors and consolidate learning.

items.prompt: How does spaced study differ from cramming?
items.answer: Study opportunities are distributed across time
distractors: Every topic is studied only once
All study occurs in one uninterrupted block
items.explanation: Spacing provides repeated opportunities for retrieval and consolidation over time rather than one concentrated session.

items.prompt: Which goal is most useful for planning an adolescent learner's next study session?
items.answer: Explain and solve three fraction-equivalence examples, then check errors
distractors: Become perfect at every subject instantly
items.explanation: A specific achievable goal names the capability and evidence, helping the learner plan and assess progress.

items.prompt: A learner mistakes fluent rereading for mastery. What would provide stronger evidence?
items.answer: Explain the idea and answer a new question without consulting notes
items.explanation: Independent explanation and transfer reveal understanding more directly than repeated exposure alone.

items.prompt: What makes formative feedback actionable?
items.answer: It identifies a gap and a feasible next step tied to the task
distractors: It compares the learner's worth with friends
items.explanation: Actionable feedback directs an improvement and should be followed by an opportunity to use it.

items.prompt: Why is private feedback sometimes preferable for a sensitive performance issue?
items.answer: It can protect dignity and support a focused conversation
distractors: It prevents the learner from receiving any feedback
items.explanation: Respectful private discussion can address concerns without unnecessary public embarrassment; transparency about criteria remains important.

items.prompt: What is a mastery-oriented classroom goal?
items.answer: Improve understanding and competence through practice and feedback
items.explanation: Mastery goals emphasize learning progress; they do not remove standards or the need for evidence.

items.prompt: Which statement reflects a useful view of ability during learning?
items.answer: Skills can improve with appropriate strategies, practice and support
distractors: Every difficulty proves a permanent inability
Effort alone guarantees success regardless of strategy
items.explanation: Development requires effective methods and opportunities; effort matters but should be connected to strategy and evidence.

items.prompt: A learner repeatedly fails a difficult task. What is the best instructional next step?
items.answer: Diagnose prerequisites and provide targeted support before further practice
distractors: Assign the same task indefinitely without feedback
items.explanation: Repeated failure can indicate gaps or unsuitable support; diagnosis should guide the next learning opportunity.

items.prompt: Why should assessment use more than one source of evidence when practical?
items.answer: A single task may not capture understanding across contexts
distractors: Every observation is equally valid automatically
All learners must submit identical answers
items.explanation: Several well-aligned observations can improve interpretation, while each source still needs appropriate criteria.

items.prompt: Which example is an access support rather than an unrelated lowering of the learning goal?
items.answer: An accessible text format while retaining the reasoning objective
distractors: Awarding full marks without any work
Removing the concept from the task entirely
Scoring only handwriting in a reasoning task
items.explanation: Access supports help learners demonstrate the intended capability without irrelevant barriers.

items.prompt: How should classroom examples represent social and cultural identities?
items.answer: Use varied respectful examples without presenting one group as inherently inferior
distractors: Assume every family has identical resources
items.explanation: Representation influences belonging and interpretation; examples should broaden participation rather than impose stereotypes.

items.prompt: Why should a teacher distinguish home-language proficiency from subject understanding?
items.answer: Language demands can obscure what a learner knows
distractors: Using another home language proves low ability
Only one language can express reasoning
Content knowledge never depends on prior experience
items.explanation: A language barrier and a conceptual gap require different support; multilingual learners may understand more than one assessment format reveals.

items.prompt: Which practice can help a hesitant multilingual learner join discussion?
items.answer: Provide preparation time and supportive ways to express reasoning
distractors: Require instant public responses in every case
items.explanation: Preparation and supportive participation options can reduce language-related pressure while preserving meaningful cognitive engagement.

items.prompt: What is a constructive purpose of classroom debate?
items.answer: Examine claims, evidence and alternative perspectives
items.explanation: Debate is educational when reasoning and respectful response are evaluated rather than personal attacks.

items.prompt: Why should learners be asked to justify an answer?
items.answer: Reasons reveal assumptions and understanding beyond the chosen option
distractors: Longer answers are always more correct
Every wrong option indicates identical misconceptions
Justification eliminates the need for subject knowledge
items.explanation: Explanations help distinguish sound reasoning from guessing and locate the specific source of an error.

items.prompt: What should a learner do when reliable evidence contradicts an initial explanation?
items.answer: Revise the explanation while examining the evidence
distractors: Treat revision as proof of personal failure
items.explanation: Revising a claim in response to evidence is part of inquiry and does not require abandoning critical evaluation of sources.

items.prompt: Which digital-literacy question helps evaluate an online claim?
items.answer: Who produced it, what evidence supports it and can credible sources corroborate it?
distractors: How many exclamation marks does it contain?
Does it agree with every prior belief?
items.explanation: Source, evidence and corroboration are stronger criteria than visual appeal or agreement with expectations.

items.prompt: Why is sharing a classmate's personal information online without permission problematic?
items.answer: It can violate privacy and cause harm
distractors: Online information can never affect anyone
items.explanation: Digital citizenship includes respecting others' privacy and using school reporting procedures for concerns.

items.prompt: What is a suitable response to suspected cyberbullying involving students?
items.answer: Preserve relevant evidence safely and follow school safeguarding procedures
distractors: Forward the harmful material to everyone
items.explanation: An appropriate response focuses on support, evidence and established procedures rather than escalating exposure or retaliation.

items.prompt: What is self-regulation in a learning context?
items.answer: Managing goals, attention, strategies and responses while learning
items.explanation: Self-regulation includes planning, monitoring and adjustment, and can be strengthened through explicit instruction and practice.

items.prompt: A student is overwhelmed by a large assignment. Which support is most appropriate?
items.answer: Break it into meaningful stages with checkpoints and feedback
items.explanation: Chunking and checkpoints help manage cognitive and organizational demands while keeping the overall goal clear.

items.prompt: Which classroom response supports emotional regulation during a disagreement?
items.answer: Pause, acknowledge feelings and guide respectful problem solving
items.explanation: Regulation includes recognizing emotions and choosing constructive responses, rather than suppressing all feelings or escalating conflict.

items.prompt: Why should a teacher avoid diagnosing a learner from one classroom incident?
items.answer: An incident lacks the context and expertise needed for diagnosis
distractors: One behaviour always proves a disorder
Diagnosis is identical to a low test score
items.explanation: Teachers can observe and refer concerns through appropriate channels without making unsupported clinical conclusions.

items.prompt: Which response is appropriate to a learner expressing persistent distress?
items.answer: Listen respectfully and connect the learner with the school's appropriate support procedures
distractors: Promise that no adult will ever be informed under any circumstances
items.explanation: Support should follow safeguarding procedures and professional roles; confidentiality has limits where safety obligations apply.

items.prompt: Why should adolescents practise evaluating consequences of choices?
items.answer: It supports more deliberate decision making in real situations
distractors: It guarantees every future choice will be perfect
It eliminates the influence of context
It requires the teacher to choose every action forever
items.explanation: Considering likely outcomes, alternatives and values helps develop judgment while recognizing uncertainty and support needs.

items.prompt: What is perspective taking?
items.answer: Considering how a situation may appear to another person
distractors: Assuming all people have identical experiences
items.explanation: Perspective taking supports understanding and communication without requiring uncritical agreement.

items.prompt: Which response to a harmful stereotype best supports critical thinking?
items.answer: Ask for evidence, examine counterexamples and discuss its effects respectfully
distractors: Repeat it as an unquestionable fact
Apply it to grade every learner
items.explanation: Stereotypes make unsupported generalizations; evidence and respectful examination help learners challenge them.

items.prompt: Why should participation expectations be explicit in a secondary classroom?
items.answer: They help learners understand how to contribute and listen fairly
distractors: They remove the need for respectful conduct
They permit only one learner to speak all year
items.explanation: Clear expectations can support inclusive discussion and make both speaking and listening responsibilities visible.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of a reflective learning journal?
items.answer: Examine strategies, difficulties and next steps using specific evidence
items.explanation: Reflection is useful when it connects experience with reasons and planned changes rather than only descriptions.

items.prompt: How can a teacher scaffold a challenging explanation task?
items.answer: Model the reasoning, provide prompts and gradually reduce support
items.explanation: Scaffolding helps learners perform with support and move toward greater independence as competence develops.

items.prompt: Why should support be reduced when a learner can perform independently?
items.answer: It encourages independent use of the skill
distractors: It proves the original support was useless
It removes the need to monitor progress
It means no future feedback is allowed
items.explanation: Support should respond to current needs; fading it allows learners to take over the reasoning and execution.

items.prompt: Which evidence best indicates transfer of learning?
items.answer: Applying a principle appropriately in a new situation and explaining why it fits
distractors: Repeating the original answer verbatim only
items.explanation: Transfer requires identifying relevant relationships across contexts rather than relying on identical surface wording.

items.prompt: Why can comparing two solution methods deepen learning?
items.answer: It reveals assumptions, efficiency and conditions of use
distractors: It proves every method works in every problem
It eliminates the need to solve either example
items.explanation: Comparison is useful when learners explain similarities, differences and why each method is appropriate.

items.prompt: How should a teacher use students' questions during a lesson?
items.answer: Treat them as evidence of interests, prior knowledge and possible gaps
distractors: Answer only the most confident student
items.explanation: Questions can guide clarification and planning, while classroom routines help manage time and participation.

items.prompt: What does learner agency involve?
items.answer: Having meaningful opportunities to influence and take responsibility for learning
distractors: Only selecting the classroom wall colour
items.explanation: Agency combines voice and purposeful action with responsibility and support, rather than unrestricted choice alone.

items.prompt: What is the SI unit of force?
items.answer: Newton
items.explanation: Force is measured in newtons; a newton is equivalent to kg·m/s².

items.prompt: What is the SI unit of energy?
items.answer: Joule
items.explanation: A joule measures energy or work. A watt measures the rate of energy transfer.

items.prompt: What is the SI unit of power?
items.answer: Watt
items.explanation: Power is energy transferred per unit time; one watt equals one joule per second.

items.prompt: What does speed measure?
items.answer: Distance travelled per unit time
distractors: Change in temperature per unit time
items.explanation: Speed is distance divided by elapsed time. Velocity also includes direction.

items.prompt: What does acceleration measure?
items.answer: Change in velocity per unit time
items.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity and can result from changing speed or direction.

items.prompt: What is inertia?
items.answer: Resistance to a change in state of motion
distractors: The total charge on a proton
items.explanation: Inertia describes the tendency to retain rest or uniform motion unless a net external force acts.

items.prompt: What is the approximate value of gravitational acceleration near Earth's surface?
items.answer: 9.8 m/s²
items.explanation: Near the surface, gravitational acceleration is approximately 9.8 m/s²; it varies slightly with location.

items.prompt: Which quantity is a vector?
items.answer: Force
items.explanation: A vector has magnitude and direction. Force and displacement are examples.

items.prompt: Which quantity is scalar?
items.answer: Mass
items.explanation: Mass has magnitude but no direction; the other listed quantities are vectors.

items.prompt: What does pressure equal?
items.answer: Force divided by area
items.explanation: Pressure is normal force per unit area, measured in pascals in SI.

items.prompt: Which relation states Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature?
items.answer: V = IR
items.explanation: Potential difference equals current times resistance under the conditions in which Ohm's law applies.

items.prompt: Which instrument measures electric current?
items.answer: Ammeter
items.explanation: An ammeter measures current and is ordinarily connected in series with the branch being measured.

items.prompt: Which instrument measures potential difference?
items.answer: Voltmeter
items.explanation: A voltmeter measures potential difference between two points and is connected across them.

items.prompt: Which arrangement gives appliances the same supply voltage in a typical household circuit?
items.answer: Parallel connection
distractors: One open circuit for all appliances
A circuit without a return path
items.explanation: In parallel branches, appliances have the same potential difference and can operate independently.

items.prompt: Which mirror is commonly used as a vehicle rear-view mirror for a wider field of view?
items.answer: Convex mirror
distractors: Plane mirror only in every case
items.explanation: A convex mirror gives an erect diminished image and a wider field of view.

items.prompt: Which lens can converge parallel light rays?
items.answer: Convex lens
items.explanation: A convex lens can converge parallel rays to a focus under ordinary conditions.

items.prompt: Why can sound not travel through an ideal vacuum?
items.answer: It requires a material medium
items.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and requires particles of a medium to carry the disturbance.

items.prompt: What is the unit of frequency?
items.answer: Hertz
items.explanation: One hertz means one cycle per second.

items.prompt: Which subatomic particle has a negative electric charge?
items.answer: Electron
items.explanation: Electrons carry negative charge; protons are positive and neutrons have no net charge.

items.prompt: What does the atomic number represent?
items.answer: Number of protons in the nucleus
distractors: Number of chemical bonds in every compound
items.explanation: The atomic number identifies an element by its proton count.

items.prompt: What are isotopes?
items.answer: Atoms of the same element with different neutron counts
distractors: Atoms with identical protons and neutrons but different names
items.explanation: Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron count and therefore mass number.

items.prompt: Which pH value indicates an acidic aqueous solution at ordinary conditions?
items.explanation: A pH below 7 is acidic at ordinary classroom conditions; pH 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline.

items.prompt: What are the usual products of acid-base neutralization?
items.answer: Salt and water
items.explanation: An acid and a base commonly react to form a salt and water; specific chemistry depends on the reactants.

items.prompt: What is the chemical formula of common salt?
items.answer: NaCl
items.explanation: Common salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.

items.prompt: What is the chemical formula of water?
items.answer: H2O
items.explanation: A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

items.prompt: Which gas is commonly released when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
items.answer: Carbon dioxide
items.explanation: Acids react with carbonates to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

items.prompt: What is rusting mainly an example of?
items.answer: Oxidation of iron in the presence of moisture and oxygen
distractors: Melting of iron without chemical change
items.explanation: Rusting is a chemical change involving iron, oxygen and water.

items.prompt: Which process separates an insoluble solid from a liquid?
items.answer: Filtration
items.explanation: A filter retains insoluble particles while the liquid passes through.

items.prompt: Which process can separate water from a salt solution and collect the water?
items.answer: Distillation
items.explanation: Distillation vaporizes water and condenses it separately; ordinary filtration does not remove dissolved salt.

items.prompt: What is a catalyst?
items.answer: A substance that changes reaction rate without being consumed overall
distractors: A reactant always used up completely
A substance that always stops every reaction
items.explanation: A catalyst participates in intermediate steps but is regenerated overall and changes the reaction pathway.

items.prompt: Which is a physical change?
items.answer: Melting ice
items.explanation: Melting changes state without changing water's chemical identity.

items.prompt: Which is a chemical change?
items.answer: Burning magnesium
items.explanation: Burning magnesium forms a new substance, magnesium oxide; the others are physical changes.

items.prompt: What is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms?
items.answer: Cell
items.explanation: Cells are the basic units of life; tissues and organs are built from cells.

items.prompt: Which cell structure controls most activities and contains chromosomes in a typical eukaryotic cell?
items.answer: Nucleus
items.explanation: The nucleus contains most genetic material and contributes to regulation of cellular activities.

items.prompt: Which organelle is especially associated with aerobic cellular respiration?
items.answer: Mitochondrion
items.explanation: Mitochondria perform major stages of aerobic respiration and ATP production.

items.prompt: Which pigment helps capture light energy for photosynthesis?
items.answer: Chlorophyll
items.explanation: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light used in photosynthesis.

items.prompt: Which plant tissue mainly transports water and mineral ions from roots?
items.answer: Xylem
items.explanation: Xylem conducts water and mineral ions; phloem transports sugars and other organic solutes.

items.prompt: Which plant tissue mainly transports sugars from sources to sinks?
items.answer: Phloem
items.explanation: Phloem moves photosynthetic products toward parts that use or store them.

items.prompt: Which gas is released during oxygenic photosynthesis?
items.answer: Oxygen
items.explanation: Oxygen is released from the splitting of water during oxygenic photosynthesis.

items.prompt: Where does most absorption of digested nutrients occur in humans?
items.answer: Small intestine
items.explanation: The small intestine has a large absorptive surface formed by folds, villi and microvilli.

items.prompt: What is the principal role of red blood cells?
items.answer: Transporting oxygen
items.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen and supports its transport.

items.prompt: Which blood components help with clotting?
items.answer: Platelets
items.explanation: Platelets contribute to forming a clot together with plasma clotting factors.

items.prompt: Which organs filter blood and form urine?
items.answer: Kidneys
items.explanation: Kidneys filter plasma and adjust water and solute balance while forming urine.

items.prompt: Which hormone helps lower elevated blood glucose?
items.answer: Insulin
items.explanation: Insulin promotes cellular uptake and storage of glucose; this is a basic biology concept, not personal treatment advice.

items.prompt: Which nutrient is a major structural material for growth and tissue repair?
items.answer: Protein
items.explanation: Proteins provide amino acids used to build and maintain tissues; a balanced diet supplies several nutrient groups.

items.prompt: Which disease is classically associated with severe vitamin C deficiency?
items.answer: Scurvy
items.explanation: Scurvy is associated with vitamin C deficiency; other deficiencies cause different conditions.

items.prompt: Which vitamin deficiency is classically associated with rickets in children?
items.answer: Vitamin D
items.explanation: Vitamin D contributes to calcium regulation and bone mineralization; severe deficiency can lead to rickets.

items.prompt: What is pollination?
items.answer: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
items.explanation: Pollination precedes fertilization in flowering plants and can occur through biotic or abiotic agents.

items.prompt: What is an ecosystem?
items.answer: Organisms interacting with one another and their physical environment
distractors: Only the top layer of soil
items.explanation: An ecosystem includes biotic components and abiotic conditions together with their interactions.

items.prompt: Which organism is a producer in a typical terrestrial food chain?
items.answer: Green plant
items.explanation: Green plants capture energy through photosynthesis; consumers and decomposers have different ecological roles.

items.prompt: A runner covers 120 metres in 20 seconds at uniform speed. What is the speed?
items.answer: 6 m/s
items.explanation: Divide distance by time: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 metres per second.

items.prompt: A car's velocity changes from 5 m/s to 17 m/s in 4 seconds. What is its average acceleration?
items.answer: 3 m/s²
items.explanation: Average acceleration is change in velocity divided by time: (17 − 5) ÷ 4 = 3 m/s².

items.prompt: A 2 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². What net force acts on it?
items.answer: 6 N
items.explanation: Newton's second law gives net force = mass × acceleration = 2 × 3 = 6 N.

items.prompt: An object moves at constant velocity in a straight line. What is the net force on it?
items.answer: Zero
items.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the vector sum of forces is zero; individual forces may still act.

items.prompt: A person completes one lap and returns to the starting point. What is their displacement?
items.answer: Zero
items.explanation: Displacement depends on final minus initial position. The distance travelled is nonzero but displacement is zero.

items.prompt: What does the slope of a distance-time graph represent during uniform straight-line motion?
items.answer: Speed
items.explanation: The graph slope is the change in distance divided by the change in time, which is speed.

items.prompt: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
items.answer: Signed displacement
items.explanation: Velocity integrated over time gives displacement; regions below the time axis contribute negatively.

items.prompt: A 5 N force moves an object 4 metres along the force direction. What work is done?
items.explanation: For force parallel to displacement, work = force × displacement = 5 × 4 = 20 J.

items.prompt: A 3 kg object travels at 4 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
items.explanation: Kinetic energy is one half of mass times speed squared: 0.5 × 3 × 16 = 24 J.

items.prompt: Using g = 10 m/s², what gravitational potential energy does a 2 kg object gain when raised 3 metres?
items.explanation: The gain near Earth's surface is mgh = 2 × 10 × 3 = 60 J.

items.prompt: A machine transfers 600 joules in 30 seconds. What is its average power?
items.explanation: Average power is energy divided by time: 600 ÷ 30 = 20 watts.

items.prompt: A 20 N force acts normally on an area of 0.5 m². What is the pressure?
items.answer: 40 Pa
items.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area = 20 ÷ 0.5 = 40 pascals.

items.prompt: An object has mass 200 g and volume 100 cm³. What is its density?
items.answer: 2 g/cm³
items.explanation: Density is mass per unit volume: 200 ÷ 100 = 2 grams per cubic centimetre.

items.prompt: Why does a sharp blade cut more readily than a blunt blade under the same normal force?
items.answer: Its smaller contact area produces greater pressure
items.explanation: With equal force, reducing the contact area increases pressure at the edge.

items.prompt: What mainly explains an object's apparent loss of weight when immersed in a fluid?
items.answer: An upward buoyant force
distractors: Conversion of all matter to heat
items.explanation: The fluid exerts an upward buoyant force; apparent weight is reduced while the object's mass remains.

items.prompt: Archimedes' principle relates buoyant force to which quantity?
items.answer: Weight of displaced fluid
distractors: Volume of air above the fluid only
items.explanation: Buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced by the immersed portion of the object.

items.prompt: Which mode of heat transfer can operate across empty space?
items.answer: Radiation
items.explanation: Thermal radiation is electromagnetic and can propagate through a vacuum.

items.prompt: Warm water rising within a heated vessel illustrates which heat-transfer mechanism?
items.answer: Convection
items.explanation: Convection transfers heat through bulk fluid movement, influenced by density differences.

items.prompt: Heat travelling along a metal rod mainly demonstrates which process?
items.answer: Conduction
distractors: Convection of the solid as a whole
items.explanation: Conduction transfers energy through interactions within a material without bulk transport of the rod.

items.prompt: At a fixed pressure, why can temperature remain constant while pure ice melts?
items.answer: Energy is used for the phase change
items.explanation: During melting, supplied energy changes the phase rather than increasing temperature until the transition is complete.

items.prompt: What is the angle of reflection when the angle of incidence to the normal is 35 degrees?
items.answer: 35 degrees
items.explanation: The law of reflection states that incidence and reflection angles, measured from the normal, are equal.

items.prompt: Why does a pencil partly submerged in water appear bent?
items.answer: Light refracts at the water-air boundary
distractors: Light can only move in circles
items.explanation: Light changes direction when passing obliquely between media with different refractive indices.

items.prompt: A plane mirror forms which kind of image of an ordinary object in front of it?
items.answer: Virtual, erect and the same size
distractors: Real and always behind the object
items.explanation: A plane mirror image is virtual and erect, with image distance behind the mirror equal to object distance in front.

items.prompt: Which property of a sound wave mainly determines perceived pitch?
items.answer: Frequency
items.explanation: Higher frequency generally corresponds to higher pitch; loudness is primarily associated with intensity.

items.prompt: In a medium, a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 2 m. What is its speed?
items.explanation: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 50 × 2 = 100 m/s.

items.prompt: A current of 2 A flows for 5 seconds. How much charge passes a point?
items.explanation: Charge = current × time = 2 × 5 = 10 coulombs.

items.prompt: A 6 V potential difference is applied across a 3 ohm ohmic resistor. What is the current?
items.answer: 2 A
items.explanation: Ohm's law gives current = voltage ÷ resistance = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 A.

items.prompt: What is the total resistance of 2 ohm and 4 ohm resistors connected in series?
items.answer: 6 ohms
items.explanation: Series resistances add because the same current flows through each resistor.

items.prompt: Two identical 6 ohm resistors are connected in parallel. What is their equivalent resistance?
items.answer: 3 ohms
items.explanation: For two equal parallel resistors, equivalent resistance is half of either resistance; reciprocal conductances add.

items.prompt: A device draws 2 A from a 12 V supply. What electrical power does it use?
items.explanation: Electrical power = voltage × current = 12 × 2 = 24 watts.

items.prompt: Why is a fuse placed in a circuit?
items.answer: To interrupt excessive current by melting its element
distractors: To guarantee zero resistance in every appliance
To increase the supply voltage indefinitely
items.explanation: A correctly rated fuse opens the circuit if current exceeds the level its element can safely carry.

items.prompt: Which observation shows that an electric current can have a magnetic effect?
items.answer: A compass needle deflects near a current-carrying wire
distractors: A dry stone becomes lighter in sunlight
items.explanation: A current produces a magnetic field around its conductor, which can affect a nearby compass.

items.prompt: What is the mass number of an atom with 6 protons and 7 neutrons?
items.explanation: Mass number counts nucleons: protons plus neutrons, so 6 + 7 = 13.

items.prompt: A neutral atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does it have?
items.explanation: Electrical neutrality requires equal numbers of protons and electrons.

items.prompt: An atom loses one electron without changing its nucleus. What does it become?
items.answer: A positively charged ion
items.explanation: Losing a negative charge leaves a net positive charge; the element's proton count stays unchanged.

items.prompt: What happens when a neutral atom gains an electron?
items.answer: It becomes a negative ion
distractors: Its atomic number increases by one
It becomes electrically neutral by definition
items.explanation: An added electron makes electron count exceed proton count, giving a net negative charge.

items.prompt: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
items.answer: Atoms of each element are conserved in an ordinary chemical reaction
distractors: Reactant names must have equal word lengths
Every reaction has exactly two reactants
items.explanation: Balancing coefficients accounts for the same number of each type of atom before and after the reaction.

items.prompt: Which balanced equation describes hydrogen reacting with oxygen to form water?
items.explanation: The balanced equation has four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side.

items.prompt: In a closed system, what happens to total mass during an ordinary chemical reaction?
items.answer: It remains constant
distractors: It depends only on the container's colour
items.explanation: Conservation of mass includes all reactants and products, including gases retained in the closed system.

items.prompt: A reaction releases heat to its surroundings. How is it described?
items.answer: Exothermic
items.explanation: An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, often observed as heat release.

items.prompt: A reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings. How is it described?
items.answer: Endothermic
items.explanation: An endothermic reaction requires net energy input from the surroundings.

items.prompt: Which observation alone does NOT establish that a chemical reaction occurred?
items.answer: A material is cut into smaller pieces
distractors: A new precipitate forms from solutions
A new gas evolves through reaction
A new substance with different properties forms
items.explanation: Changing size by cutting can leave chemical identity unchanged, whereas formation of new substances is evidence of reaction.

items.prompt: What is an element?
items.answer: A substance whose atoms have the same proton number
distractors: Any material with two visible layers
A mixture of any two gases
Only a substance that dissolves in water
items.explanation: An element is identified by atomic number; it cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.

items.prompt: What is a compound?
items.answer: A substance with different elements chemically combined in a fixed composition
items.explanation: Compounds have a defined chemical composition and properties distinct from those of their constituent elements.

items.prompt: Which example is a mixture rather than a pure compound?
items.answer: Air
items.explanation: Air contains several gases whose proportions can vary; its components are not one fixed chemical compound.

items.prompt: Which mixture is homogeneous at the scale of ordinary observation?
items.answer: Salt fully dissolved in water
items.explanation: A dissolved salt solution has uniform composition throughout at ordinary scales, unlike the heterogeneous alternatives.

items.prompt: What is a solute in a solution?
items.answer: The substance dissolved in the solvent
distractors: Always a gas above the liquid
items.explanation: A solute is dissolved in a solvent; both can have different physical states depending on the solution.

items.prompt: What is a saturated solution at a specified temperature?
items.answer: One containing the maximum amount of solute that can remain dissolved under those conditions
distractors: One in which every possible substance dissolves
items.explanation: Saturation refers to an equilibrium solubility limit for a particular solute and solvent under stated conditions.

items.prompt: Why can ordinary filter paper not separate dissolved sugar from water?
items.answer: Dissolved sugar passes through with the liquid
distractors: The filter removes only water molecules
items.explanation: Ordinary filtration retains sufficiently large insoluble particles; it does not remove molecularly dissolved sugar.

items.prompt: Which technique can recover solid salt from saltwater without collecting the water?
items.answer: Evaporation
distractors: Simple decantation of a uniform solution
items.explanation: Evaporating the solvent leaves nonvolatile salt behind; distillation would also collect condensed solvent.

items.prompt: Which method can separate iron filings from dry sand?
items.answer: Magnetic separation
items.explanation: A magnet attracts iron filings while ordinary sand is not strongly attracted.

items.prompt: Which technique can help separate the coloured components of an ink?
items.answer: Paper chromatography
items.explanation: Different dissolved components travel differently through the stationary phase with the mobile solvent.

items.prompt: Which change of state is sublimation?
items.answer: Solid directly to gas
items.explanation: Sublimation bypasses the liquid state; the reverse gas-to-solid change is deposition.

items.prompt: What is condensation?
items.answer: Gas changing to liquid
items.explanation: Cooling a vapour under suitable conditions can cause it to form a liquid.

items.prompt: What is evaporation?
items.answer: Liquid changing into vapour from its surface
items.explanation: Evaporation occurs at a liquid's surface and need not wait until the liquid reaches its boiling point.

items.prompt: Which condition generally increases evaporation from water at the same temperature?
items.answer: Greater exposed surface area
distractors: Reducing air movement while other factors stay equal
items.explanation: A larger surface gives more molecules an opportunity to escape; humidity and airflow also affect the rate.

items.prompt: How does blue litmus respond to a typical acidic aqueous solution?
items.answer: It turns red
distractors: It turns green in every acid
It remains blue in every acid
items.explanation: Litmus is an acid-base indicator; acids turn blue litmus red under ordinary testing conditions.

items.prompt: How does red litmus respond to a typical basic aqueous solution?
items.answer: It turns blue
distractors: It turns yellow in every base
It remains red in every base
items.explanation: Bases turn red litmus blue under ordinary testing conditions.

items.prompt: What does a higher pH generally indicate when comparing ordinary aqueous solutions?
items.answer: Lower hydrogen-ion activity
items.explanation: pH is related logarithmically to hydrogen-ion activity; increasing pH corresponds to decreasing activity.

items.prompt: Compared with pH 4, approximately how much greater is hydrogen-ion activity at pH 3?
items.answer: Ten times
items.explanation: A change of one pH unit represents a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion activity.

items.prompt: Which type of bonding involves sharing electron pairs between atoms?
items.answer: Covalent bonding
items.explanation: Covalent bonds involve shared electron pairs, while ionic bonding is associated with electrostatic attraction between ions.

items.prompt: Which attraction primarily holds the ions together in sodium chloride?
items.answer: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
distractors: A string of neutral water molecules
items.explanation: Sodium and chloride ions form an ionic lattice maintained by electrostatic interactions.

items.prompt: Why can molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
items.answer: Its ions can move and carry charge
items.explanation: Mobile ions carry current in the molten salt; ions in a solid lattice cannot move freely through it.

items.prompt: Which property is commonly associated with many metals?
items.answer: Good electrical conductivity
items.explanation: Many metals have mobile electrons that support electrical and thermal conduction, although properties vary among metals.

items.prompt: What is an alloy?
items.answer: A metallic material made by combining a metal with one or more other elements
items.explanation: Alloying can change strength, corrosion resistance and other properties; the added element need not itself be a metal.

items.prompt: What is galvanizing iron commonly intended to achieve?
items.answer: Reduce corrosion using a protective zinc coating
items.explanation: Zinc protects iron through a barrier and sacrificial corrosion behaviour when the coating is damaged.

items.prompt: Which statement about a catalyst in a reaction is correct?
items.answer: It changes reaction rate without changing the equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature
distractors: It always changes the element identities
It must be consumed as the final product
It makes conservation of atoms unnecessary
items.explanation: A catalyst changes the path and speeds approach to equilibrium; it does not change the thermodynamic equilibrium constant at a given temperature.

items.prompt: What distinguishes a reversible reaction in a closed chemical system?
items.answer: Products can react to regenerate reactants
distractors: It can only happen once in the universe
It requires all materials to be solids
items.explanation: A reversible reaction can proceed in both directions; equilibrium involves equal forward and reverse rates, not necessarily equal amounts.

items.prompt: Which structure forms the selective boundary of a cell?
items.answer: Cell membrane
items.explanation: The cell membrane regulates exchange between the cell and its surroundings through several transport mechanisms.

items.prompt: Which structure is usually present in plant cells but absent from animal cells?
items.answer: Cell wall
items.explanation: Plant cells usually have a cellulose-containing wall outside the membrane; both plant and animal cells have membranes and ribosomes.

items.prompt: Which organelle is responsible for protein synthesis?
items.answer: Ribosome
items.explanation: Ribosomes assemble amino acids into proteins using information carried by messenger RNA.

items.prompt: What is diffusion?
items.answer: Net movement from higher to lower concentration due to random particle motion
distractors: Movement requiring every particle to travel in one direction
items.explanation: Random motion continues in both directions, but a concentration difference causes net movement down the gradient.

items.prompt: What is osmosis?
items.answer: Net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane down its water-potential gradient
distractors: Movement only of proteins through air
Movement of salt without any membrane
items.explanation: Osmosis concerns water movement across a selectively permeable membrane; solutes can influence the water-potential difference.

items.prompt: What is a tissue?
items.answer: A group of cells organized to perform related functions
items.explanation: Tissues are organized cellular structures; several tissue types can contribute to one organ.

items.prompt: What is an organ system?
items.answer: A set of organs working together in a major body function
distractors: Only a colony of unrelated microbes
items.explanation: For example, digestive organs work together to process food and absorb nutrients.

items.prompt: Where does gas exchange chiefly occur in the human lungs?

items.prompt: What is the basic role of the human heart?

items.prompt: Which vessels carry blood away from the heart?

items.prompt: Which vessels carry blood toward the heart?

items.prompt: Why are capillaries important in circulation?

items.prompt: What is the role of stomata in leaves?

Fusion of male and female gametes
Digestion of starch in the mouth

A fungal spore in every case

items.prompt: Which molecule carries hereditary information in most organisms?

items.prompt: Why does sexual reproduction usually generate varied offspring?

The percentage of stones in soil

items.prompt: Why should crop spacing be appropriate for the crop and conditions?

items.prompt: What is a weed in crop production?

items.prompt: Why is early weed control often important?

items.prompt: Which soil fraction generally has the smallest mineral particles?

items.prompt: What does soil texture describe?

items.explanation: Texture refers to particle-size composition and influences physical behaviour; it differs from soil structure.

items.prompt: Why can soil organic matter support crop production?

Only a high population of insects

items.prompt: What do N, P and K denote on common fertilizer labels?

items.prompt: What is drip irrigation mainly designed to do?

Remove the crop's need for roots

items.prompt: What is the main function of field drainage?

items.prompt: Why can mulching help conserve soil moisture?

items.prompt: What is integrated pest management?
